The Illumination of the Great Way (*Mahānayaprakāśa*):
That whose nature transcends the states of succession and non-succession shines forth most intensely within the final stage of the sequence.
I bow to that indescribable Goddess, whose sole nature is the experience of the profound abyss, and whose foundation is free from the fear of obstacles. 1/1.
Although the tradition of the sequence of the wheel of great meaning is perfectly joined by the wise,
nevertheless, alas, they still practice it through reasoning.
Just as it is endowed [with its qualities], it is not lost from one's own direct experience. || 1/2 ||
That which is his own essential nature— homeless, immeasurable,
self-luminous, pure, undiminished, and supremely autonomous;
which is the soul of the universe and yet transcends it— that is his [true] state.
Bondage and liberation, it is said, are both produced by false conceptualization. (1.3)

In this way, it is impossible to realize such a reality of the self here, nor to correctly uproot the proliferation of false conceptual constructions, without abandoning the reasoning that consists of the Great Way (Mahānaya).
For it is the most supreme among all the supreme, and therefore it is of great significance. || 1/4 ||
Now, by means of the method for the comprehension of all objects, the nature of this very [work], which consists of the worldly course as it actually exists,
is being unveiled through exposition, veneration, and transmission.
The lineage of the Guru possesses an eternal and undiminished glory. || 1/5 ||
This [work], which contains the essence of experience and the core of reasoning, which brings an end to doubts arising from the mouth of the Guru,
is the internal means for the swift attainment of the supreme state.
Having reflected upon it in the heart, it is established by the great ones. || 1/6 ||
When the Śāmbhava immersion has ascended through an exceedingly intense descent of power (śaktipāta),
the entire universe manifests as the form of the nectar of one’s own bliss for one who is liberated while living.
Even as it proceeds through the distinctions of excessive, moderate, and mild [intensity], the mode of subtle scrutiny belonging to that most powerful descent of grace shines forth. (1.8)

That which is one's own innate nature, existing from time immemorial, all-pervading, and omnipresent, [is realized] through the tradition seen from the mouth of the Guru by means of the method of yoga without external means. (1.9)

Of that radiance which is one's own essential nature, which consists of the universe shining as its very being, and which remains forever distinct and unobscured throughout every state of experience— (1.10)

This very sequence, which has the Purāṇa as its foundation yet is devoid of sequence, is the supreme consummation of the Great Purpose (mahārtha), wherein the distinction between self and other has dissolved. (1.11)
May that supreme Purāṇa-adhiṣṭhāna, which is the primordial, eternally established abode of the Self, be proclaimed. 1/12

Free from the agitation of the latent impressions of distractions such as the practice of reasoning and so forth, this is the method that is without means; he in whom this is firmly established is a king among yogis. (1.13)
(3) Liberated from all obscurations and having abandoned the states of rejection and acquisition, it requires nothing else for the sake of abiding in its own essential nature. 1/14

The consciousness that rests upon the flood of cognitions, both non-conceptual and conceptual, experiences the wonder of supreme bliss through contact with that which consists of that [consciousness]. (1.15)

That Mistress of the Left, who is the elemental void, through the audacity of her glance upon the Guru, brings about purification for him everywhere, beginning with the sequence of the sacred seats (pīṭhakrama). 1.16.
Just as this universe, which cannot be denied, arises, so too does its persistence and destruction occur within its own nature, and its dissolution occurs within its essential form. (1.17)
Moreover, when this [state] exists, there arises for one whose mind is tranquilized by the moonlight of the wonder of supreme bliss a state of being free from obscuration. (1.18)
In all these matters, one proceeds free from conceptual construction;
for that which is called "knowledge" arises indeed through the grace of the Guru. (1.19)
In that state which is exceedingly firm and established in one's own direct experience, purity shines forth, transcending the sequence of verbal description and the like. (1.20)
And when this most intense [state] has been set in motion by the Guru’s instruction, it is revealed through the mere discourse of conventions regarding the seen, the unseen, and so forth. (1.21)
In states of worldly activity that are intensely intense, those [powers] manifest—arising both externally and internally—by turning toward each respective object. (1.22)
The goddesses of consciousness are the rafters shattered by the impact of the great void;
through the interruption of their worship, one's true nature is fully revealed. (1.23)
For one whose self-awareness has taken root in that which is empty of the latent impressions of conceptual construction, knowledge manifests without depending on external means. (1.24)
For some, knowledge in which the non-conceptual portion predominates manifests very gradually through conceptualization, by relying on discourse such as linguistic conventions. (1.25)
When someone is established [in practice] depending on the sequence of worship and so forth, the non-conceptual arises immediately following conceptualization. (1.26)

Regarding the state of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) when it has not yet begun to function, this sequence is declared according to its divisions, such as "excessive" (*atimātra*) and so forth. (1.27)
This sequence of the descent of power (śaktipāta), beginning with the "most intense" (mahātīvratama) and so forth, demonstrates the sovereignty of Maheśvara that has ascended to the highest level.
It is not otherwise; he is designated as such out of reverence for the Guru.
Therefore, in the sequence of Mahānaya, the word "Mahā" at the beginning possesses its proper meaning. (The reading "uhāśabda" is noted. 1/29.

In the traditions of Kulakaula and others, in the Śākta and Trika doctrines and so forth—in these extensive discourses containing secret teachings which serve as the cause for abiding in one's true nature. (1.30)
Even though there exist various divisions of Siddhānta and Tantra, as well as those consisting of other means, this Great Way (Mahānaya) remains pervasive and all-encompassing. 1.31

For those who seek the great purpose and have thoroughly examined the sequence of what precedes and what follows, there is indeed no other recourse than the courage to swallow conceptual construction. (1.32)
One who is well-awakened here is free from expectations, whereas the awakened one still expects merely the discourse on conventions and the like, as well as the worship of the wheel. (1.33)
The essential point regarding that which is merely a conventional discourse on what is seen and lost, and so forth, has been elaborated elsewhere; therefore, it will now be discussed briefly. (1.34)

This worship consists of both the non-sequential and the sequential; it is the commencement of the sequence of the sacred seats (*pīṭhakrama*), radiant with the true tradition through the application of the method for the division of the manifestation of the wheels (*cakrollāsa*). (The application of the manifestation of the [sacred] mouths.)
Lest such [a teaching] be lost here through the passage of time, we shall now fully unfold the meaning of the Guru’s words by relying upon this very [work]. (1.35)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Universal Distinctiveness," in the *Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa*.
Now begins the second chapter. (p.
5) Having bowed to the true seed of the oral tradition from the mouth of the most excellent Guru—the supreme secret [of] the nature of the Pīṭha-krama—it is first set forth. 2.1.
Relying upon the world as it truly exists, consisting of the nature of real entities, the arrangement of the *pīṭha-krama* is now described in a manner that reaches the heart. (2.2)

The expansion of the wheel of goddesses, which exists as the sequence of sacred seats (pīṭha), is declared by the Guru to be the instruction on the lineage (rajjñapti) in the form of the sequence of sacrifice and so forth. (2.3)
In this world, worldly transaction (vyavahāra) exists primarily as the nature of action;
therefore, the instruction on the sequence of the seats (pīṭhakrama) is explained by means of that very [action]. (2.4)
With this very intention, at the outset, the bound soul (paśu) is made a vessel for the tradition by the Guru, preceded by the consumption of the sacrificial pap (caru). (2.5)

For that which consists of the sacred seats (pīṭha), cremation grounds (śmaśāna), fields (kṣetra), lords (īśa), and assemblies (melaka) is indeed the Transmission of the Seats (pīṭhakrama); here, from the seats [proceed] Vyomeśvarī and the others in sequence. (2.6)

That body which consists of the aggregate of the void, the vital breaths, the intellect, the cognitive faculties, and the organs of action, and that which is insentient by nature as the external object; (2.7)
Established from the sky down to the earth, it is served by the Siddhas and Yoginīs who are the foundation for infinite experience. (2.8)
Because the rays of consciousness are seen clearly as they rely upon this place of convention, it is therefore called a *pīṭha*. (2.9)
Through the sacrifice whose nature is the organs of action, one remains established up to the end of the Void;
the sequence beginning with *udyoga* occurs within the body, externally following the order of earth and the other elements. (2.10)
In this system, the great pervasion (mahāvyāpti) exists everywhere, with each preceding element pervading each subsequent one;
moreover, the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum (āśrayāśrayibhāva) is established as being non-differentiated. (2.11)

Because it is of the nature of the night’s covering, because it is infinite, and because it is undisturbed, O Vyomeśī, the resting place of all consciousnesses is the very essence of the sacred seat (pīṭha). (2.12)
Within the body, which is empty of a self, she alone remains as that which has been recited;
that which extends to the organs of action is the expansion of consciousness, and she is its support. (2.13)
From the foundation up to the end of the earth, whatever is of the nature of insentient matter exists;
it is by virtue of being the support for this very [sentient reality] that the sky outside is considered the "seat" (pīṭha). (2.14)

That consciousness which vibrates within the sky that is not limited by time, being the sole ground for the burning away of time, is considered the Sky-farer (Khecarī) and the cremation ground (Śmaśāna). (2.15)

In the state of deep sleep, which is beyond verbal description, the vital breath (prāṇa), possessing the power of vibration, devours time within the body; therefore, it is known as the cremation ground (śmaśāna). (2.16)
Time, moreover, is brought to an end within the form of the conceptualization of the object of knowledge;
because its nature is to swallow time, that [conceptualization] is externally the cremation ground. (2.17)
This supreme field, which has reached the stage of light and bliss, is protected by the two [hands] as the Field-guardian (*kṣetrapa*) upon the earth. (2.18)

Since the cognizing subject (pramātṛ), who exists within the body, protects the field (kṣetra) consisting of the void and vital breath (śūnyaprāṇamaya), he is therefore the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa), and is composed of that very [nature]. (2.19)

Even with respect to external objects, the element of fire, whose nature is the sphere of the sky, protects the field; therefore, by virtue of having that as its essence, she herself is that [fire]. (2/20)

That knowledge consisting of the manifestation of all things which has entered into supreme consciousness by way of its essential nature as equilibrium—that indeed is the *mela*, the devourer of dissolution. (2.21)
The withdrawal of appearances is that state of abiding within another light;
it occurs through a complete turning back by means of the nature of equilibrium. (2.22)
Because she consumes through internal contact, she is the "Devourer of Withdrawal" (saṃhārabhakṣiṇī).
[She is] nourished by the wonder arising from the enjoyment of sense objects. (2.23)
Where knowledge consisting of the appearance of the intellect and the senses subsides, there occurs a smooth union with the inner self in the form of the state of the seed. (2/24)
When this [mind], free from mental constructs, is capable of receiving a reflection, it experiences itself through the blending of the relish of internal equanimity. (2.25)

The state [of the Self] exists as the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), impulses (*vedha*), and residual traces (*saṃskāra*), because it is being struck with intensity and serves as the cause for supreme satisfaction. (2/26)

Agitated by swarms of bees driven away by the great roar from within the Fullness, she is oriented toward the state of rest in her own self, which is difficult to perceive due to the absence of veils. (2/27)

That which consists of the primordial descent of power (*ādyāyāmala*), whose ground is profound and vast, is the sacrifice to Raudrī and Raudreśvarī; therefore, it is desired by the most excellent gurus. (2.28)
This is the transition into a complete swallow, the birthplace of great audacity; it is characterized by a forced union due to the meeting with one who is exceedingly dear. (2.29)
Even those entities within the body that are clearly manifested through the organs of action are forgotten at that moment, due to the complete cessation of desire for them. (2.30)
This sacrifice, which finds its rest within the internal realization witnessed by oneself—herein the conformity of this Goddess is clearly perceived. (2.31)
That earth which is perceived by her as external is dependent upon various actions;
it is that sacrifice wherein all things immediately find their rest. (2.32)

In this way, having resorted through the sequence of the seats (*pīṭha*) to the state of being an object of knowledge—the nature of which consists of the conscious and the insentient, appearing as the form of the cremation ground—the wheel of goddesses unfolds. (2.33)
Because it is all-pervasive in nature, because it is thus directly perceived, because it is the foundation of everything from beginning to end, and because it is the most supreme of all. (2.34)

Because it possesses the nature of all-enduring power, because it is the cause of favoring others, and because it consists merely of the highest praise, the pedestal is designated as the Praṇava. (2.35)
As this sequence of the Great Wheel is being described in its proper order, there occurred within it a manifest experience of the Lord of the Eye. (2.36)
Then that meditation was contemplated as that external seat, the best of all seats, frequented by yoginīs and siddhas, situated in the northern direction. (2.37)
The body of the sequence of the abodes (dhāmakrama) has also been described within [the body] itself, established as the support of all gnoses for the sake of worldly conduct. (2.38)
Wherever these goddesses of consciousness—who are the essence of pervasion—fall, whether within or without, that is proclaimed to be the sacred abode (dhāman). (2.39)
If there exists here some other subtle darkness of doubt before the eye of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it will itself be dispelled. (2.40)
The oral tradition of the *pīṭhakrama* is said to consist solely of the experience of perceiving the objects of the body;
those whose hearts are fixed on this very [tradition] bring about dissolution.
The net of existence and liberation is produced by false conceptualization. // 2.41 //
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Pīṭhas," in the Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa.

Now begins the third chapter. Having bowed to that state wherein there is repose in its own nature through the contraction and expansion of [the powers of] arising, manifestation, time, and grasping— [and] by virtue of those causes— (3/1).
We describe the circle of Vyomeśvarī as having a phenomenal nature that is beautiful and sublime through the logic of the vibration of the universal manifestation from its very root. (3.2)

Regarding that wheel of rays which is manifest and established within the sequence of the seats (pīṭha), its configuration from the root upward is described by means of the nature of consciousness (saṃvidātmanā). (3/3)
Indeed, this entire universe that exists, consisting of the fivefold group beginning with sound, cannot be denied, because it is established by one's own self-awareness. (3.4)
Its establishment as something external to consciousness cannot be achieved in any way;
for without its being of the nature of cognition, even its externality is not established. (3.5)
Therefore, in the world, the state of being an external self exists in dependence upon the body;
for even an omniscient one would find it difficult to perceive that [body] as something separate from consciousness. (3.6)
Therefore, the existence of the entire universe depends in every respect upon consciousness;
because of the preeminence of knowledge, it is established that there is neither illusion (māyā) nor mental impression (vāsanā). (3.7)
(10) It is free from the anxieties of [limitations such as] direction, place, time, form, and so forth;
even while being the essence of the conceivable universe, it remains transcendent of it. (3.8)
Surely consciousness, consisting of the universe, exists because it is experienced by everyone;
yet at that time, there is no experience of its nature as transcending that [universe]. (3.9)
If it were to expand first, how indeed would it expand as pure consciousness alone?
For how could the state of being the self of the universe belong to consciousness whose nature is free from all veils? (3.10)

If the excellence of manifestation were not of the nature of blue—that is, if it were not essentially blue—then the manifestation of blue would not occur at all, by virtue of the power of the self-awareness [of that manifestation]. (3.11)
Therefore, that which is the manifestation of blue consists essentially of the excellence of blue;
since its manifestation as non-different from blue is established, blueness itself is also experienced. (3.12)
If its manifestation were of a single nature, the concealment of the blue would be impossible;
even if it were external to the manifestation, this same logic applies, for it is distinct from it. (3.13)

The manifestation of the diversity of the universe results from the variety of the causes that are latent impressions (vāsanā), and not from the mere unfolding of the manifestation whose nature is pure. (3.14)
The statement "the universe is that which is manifesting" is thus justified;
for the universe is indeed manifestation itself, as established by the experience of all. (3.15)
But the light that transcends the universe is not experienced as independent; therefore, even this self-manifestation is established as being governed by the universe. (3.16)
To this it is replied: As for what was said—how can consciousness that transcends the universe enter and be perceived within the plane of universal experience? (3.17)
For at the time of the experience of blue, there manifests a manifestation whose nature is non-conceptual supreme I-consciousness, free from the coloring of the form of blue. (3.18)

Even in the state of conceptualization (*savikalpadaśā*), there is no experience of distinction among cognitions of pleasure, blue, and so forth; thus, there is no dispute regarding their internal or external nature. (3.19)

In the very same way, although it is non-different from the experience of blue, that inward-turned light which remains established as the nature of supreme subjectivity (parāhantā) is abandoned by it. (3.20)
Through *hevāka* alone is he perceived by other knowers of reality;
otherwise, even the cognition of blue would not be established. (3.21)
Since the existence of consciousness is not admitted without an appearance, how indeed could even an appearance be established without consciousness? (3.22)
For in this way, the cognition of blue is not established through mutual dependence; rather, here the existence of cognitions must be understood as independent of any external manifestation. (3.23)
Since independence and dependence are ineffective in this regard, they are not capable of establishing the established fact of the experience of blue. (3.24)
Prior to its establishment, the state of dependence is equal for both the blue object and its manifestation;
once established, the state of independence is equal for both the blue object and its manifestation. (3.25)
Now, blue cannot manifest by depending on another, for manifestation does not [arise] again [in that way];
because its nature is self-manifestation, blue depends upon itself. (3.26)
Therefore, blue is dependent, whereas its manifestation is considered independent.
Since both dependence and independence are ineffective in that regard, how [can they be established]? (3.27)

It is understood that just as blue, although produced from causes, is said to be dependent on other factors in relation to its manifestation (*prakāśa*), and not in terms of its own nature (*rūpa*). (3.28)
Blue exists as blue within its own nature, but not as something independent within the nature of manifestation;
for light, however, does not exist apart from mere manifestation. (3/29)
In that much alone, it is not logical for manifestation to depend upon blue;
however, in the case of the nature of blue itself, there is in every respect a dependence upon the manifestation of blue. (3/30)
For the form of blue is established as being essentially blue by virtue of its own cause;
it is not, however, essentially luminous, since it is generally perceived by the blind and others. (3.31)

But when that which is of the nature of light has arisen—consisting in the manifestation of both self and other—and is established according to experience, all dependence [on external means] ceases. (3.32)
In that case, blue does not depend upon manifestation for its own establishment;
however, manifestation depends upon blue within itself for its apprehension. (3/33)
In this way, the dependence of luminosity would manifest all the more;
for its arising is not admitted to be devoid of manifestation. (3.34)

Now, [one might object]: "In the manifestation of blue, that aspect of manifestation which is established—how could it have a dependence upon the blue for the sake of its own ontological existence? (3/35)
The attainment of its own nature arises from the preceding aspect, which is of the nature of the cause;
therein, there is no dependence on "blue," because consciousness exists through its own self-luminosity. (3.36)
Insofar as the blue portion has the nature of manifestation, it actually possesses a dependence upon manifestation;
for this very [dependence] is characterized by autonomy and heteronomy. (3/37)
In this way, what could have been meant by this? Is it with attributes (sopādhi) or without attributes (nirupādhi)? Is it the innate nature of the Light itself, or is it of both natures? (3.38)

If [the nature] were with conditions, then because of the mutual dependence between the condition and that [nature], neither would be established; how, then, could a nature possessing conditions be established? (3/39)
Now, if that form is without attributes, how can there be the manifestation of an attribute?
Since the Supreme cannot reside in another, the existence of the world would thus be undermined. (3.40)
(13) Now, if it is argued that the form which consists of both [aspects]— though accompanied by limiting adjuncts— is yet devoid of them,
and thus everything is perfectly consistent, then let it be perceived as such.
In that state, how can there be the experience of a form that is free from limiting adjuncts (anupādhi), while one remains on the non-conceptual ground whose nature is self-awareness? (3.42)

Nor should there be a denial [of this], because it would entail the same faults as previously mentioned; nor can that which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) be known as a constituent part of the blue [object]. (3/43)
Therefore, that which consists of the supreme *ahantā* is considered non-conventional (*asāṅketika*).
This is what was described as the direct perception (*pratyakṣabheda*) whose nature is self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). (3.44)

In that case, if this [distinction] is not based on intention (*āśaya*), what is the basis for its differentiation? Surely, according to the analogy of water colored by lac, how could there even be memory for you? (3.45)
For the single, ultimate form consists of blood and water;
conceptual construction, however, divides it specifically according to its own creative power. (3.46)
In the same way, the nature of the manifestation of blue exists as an undivided whole;
it is only through the artifice of conceptual construction that fragmentation occurs therein. (3.47)
From a manifestation that is undifferentiated in nature, and from a cause of exactly that same kind, there proceeds a continuous succession of an effect of precisely that same kind. (3/48)
However, defects such as mutual dependence and the like are considered to be contingent;
how could they possibly arise in that case where [the two] are established in non-conceptuality? (3.49)
It is understood, however, that this logic regarding the identity of blue and its manifestation is flawed;
for while their oneness might follow from their non-opposition, how could there be oneness between the insentient and the sentient? (3.50)
Light that is partless and self-luminous is considered real; whereas light that has parts and depends on the manifestation of another is considered unreal. (3.51)
If there were absolute identity, the distinction between the real and the unreal would be lost;
since it possesses both a unitary and a manifold nature, its intrinsic nature is not extinguished. (3.52)
But since the negation of intrinsic nature is sublated by experience, that self-established manifestation must become the cause for the determination of other things. (3.53)
Therefore, even though it is indivisible, the non-difference between the blue object and its manifestation must be accepted; how then could the analogy of the red water be applicable here? (3.54)

Furthermore, if there were an actual non-difference between the blue object and its manifestation, how could a manifestation that has become liberation occur through the disappearance of the appearance from that which is transparent? (3.55)

Its nature is a beginningless flow; it is the essence of the states of being a knower, an agent, and the capacity for action. Furthermore, there exists no other real causal complex for manifestation and latent impressions.
For it is by means of that [knowledge] that the destruction of latent impressions occurs, even in the absence of illumination. (3.58)

At the time of liberation from that [state], what is desired by the knowers of reality as the cessation of appearances does not occur for one who has not yet attained [the state], because its own cause remains incomplete and uninterrupted. (3.59)
In that regard, whatever is conceptualized as the purity of the substratum and so forth does not, by way of reasoning, result in being the seed of omniscience. (3/60)
Therefore, knowledge conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) cannot attain stability, even if there is identity [between the object and its cognition], because of their mutual dependence. (3.61)
And as for that light which is of the nature of pure consciousness and self-established, how could it extend even in the slightest degree toward an adjunct? (3.62)
And that which has not entered into cognition would not exist even if it were identical [to it], just as a jewel is not the object of the cognition [of] silver and the like. (3.63)
With this very intention, it has been stated by those skilled in the reality of reasoning:
"Even though a crystal or similar object is colored by the light of an external object, it is comparable to a clod of earth [or, rather, comparable to something insentient]. (3.64)
Now, at the time of the manifestation of blue, how can the excellence of the very nature of blue—which consists of a manifestation dependent on another—be denied? (3.65)
If it is additional, how does it appear? If it appears, how can it be additional?
That "it appears" and "it is additional" are mutually inconsistent. (3/66)
In that case, there would be only pure light, free from limiting adjuncts and untainted;
and thus, the world-order, consisting of manifold experiences, would perish. (3.67)
To this it is replied: that which exceeds [the limited] manifestation is first of all established by reasoning.
When the emergence of the world is manifested through the power of its own internal representation, then its own nature is one of uninterrupted form. (3.69)

The universe consists of the manifestation of consciousness and is established within that manifestation of consciousness; it does not exceed the manifestation of consciousness, yet it accomplishes the course of worldly life. (3.70)

And this mention (ullekha), which consists of reflective awareness (vimarśa) and is fashioned from one's own manifestation, is considered by the wise to be the ultimate establishment of the object. (3.71)
This very radiance of consciousness, whose essence is the nature of the Great Being, consists of the core agency of its own self-inscription; it exists as an object of direct experience. (3.72)
This universe, consisting of the power of its own self-reflection, manifests by its very nature as if emerging, unbroken, due to its absolute freedom. (3.73)

And because it arises from an experience consisting of the bliss of an undivided object, it is that [state] which, by virtue of its essence being pure consciousness, abides everywhere in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*). (3.74)

If there were a difference in the knowledge residing within the self due to the distinctions of diversity in direction, place, and time as taught in the Bhāgavata, then how could that [diversity] be manifested? (3.75)
Therefore, because of the incapacity for manifestation, that distinction is not established; nor is a distinction experienced even within the appearance through a further division into parts. (3.76)

Due to ignorance, which is like a heap of sesame seeds, or because of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have become integrated, the uniformity of the manifestation is established [as primary] from the very beginning. (3.77)
Furthermore, it is this very consciousness of the manifold that appears;
though its conceptual proliferation is distinct, it is incapable of knowing that [consciousness] as it truly is. (3.78)

Neither individually nor collectively can they differentiate its own nature, because such a state is not established by experience; how then could there be a simultaneous manifestation of them? (3.79)
Likewise, if consciousness consists of the universe as a single unity, how can there be its manifestation?
And by being constrained by that [manifestation], its oneness is lost. (3.80)
Even when all-pervading, that consciousness is free from the coloring of various forms;
because its nature is indivisible experience, it abides in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya). || 3/81 ||
This freedom from agitation, as well as this profound and noble character—this is that sovereignty so difficult to achieve, possessing an extraordinary nature. (3.82)
When a form appears through consciousness itself, no error exists;
for it is held that error consists in the manifestation of one thing by means of the support of another. (3.83)

The manifestation of its own light is not erroneous, because it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). This establishment through self-awareness is not sublated in any way whatsoever. (3/84)
Because there is no second moon externally, [the cognition] subsequent to that sublation occurs;
for indeed, in the experience of two moons, its life consists solely in mere appearance. (3/85)
If there were a sublation of that which consists of self-awareness, then because it is of a single, non-dual nature, even the sublation itself would be sublated. (3.86)
Therefore, the Goddess of Consciousness, consisting of her own internal representation and characterized by self-awareness, creates the painting of the universe upon her own screen. (3.87)

Neither illusory manifestation (vivarta) nor transformation (pariṇāma), nor anything else, exists apart from consciousness, since the emergence of the universe occurs through the power of the conceptualization of the unreal and so forth. (3.88)

Nor could the manifold variety of the universe consist of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*), as is the case with the supernatural powers and insights of one possessed of profound and noble consciousness. (3.89)
That form, being delineated by means of names and beautified by the diversity of those names, emerges like foam from consciousness and unfolds through its own inherent power. (3.90)
Relying upon such absolute freedom of consciousness, it is possible to establish that the entire collection of objects of knowledge exists as ultimately real. (3.91)
Relying upon the nature of direct perception and consisting of the experience of objects, the form of consciousness (cidrūpa) concordant with Mahānaya has been set forth. (3/92)
Since there is much more that could be said regarding this object of knowledge, we desist; only a mere indication has been revealed. (3.93)
Some cognitions have a support, while others are without a support;
even among those, there is a diversity based on being conceptual or non-conceptual. (3.94)
Even there, there is great variety consisting of both the determinate and the indeterminate;
and even therein, the expansion of knowledge and the objects of knowledge has many levels. (3.95)

(18) Due to the connection with results corresponding to the web of actions based on faith or lack of faith, there too arise infinite delusions of mind, such as [rebirth in] heaven, hell, and so forth. (3/96)
In that [reality], even the distinctions between bondage and liberation are not ultimately real;
likewise, the infinite configurations of the world and their origins are of such a nature. (3.97)
Likewise, having transcended the stage of the mind (*manobhūmi*) which is still coagulating, one passes beyond it;
this is considered the manifestation of that very portion of consciousness which has become fully solidified. (3.98)

And that [reality] consists of the nature of non-conceptual, innate, effortless self-reflection; it consists of the solidification of the essence of free consciousness, which is of a single, transparent form. (3.99)

One immerses oneself in the nature of consciousness—which is infinite, unfathomable, and profound—wherein there is the penetration of the states of succession and non-succession, and which is adorned with intuitive flash (*pratibhā*). (3.100)
This form of the Lord is both the universal self and that which is other than it;
it transcends existence and non-existence, and is both the support of all and itself without support. (3.101)

Even though its nature is the illumination of that which was unilluminated, it would be improper—indeed, quite contrary to reason—for that [consciousness] to exist by its own inherent nature without the Supreme Power (parā śakti). (3.102)

Because it does not find a firm footing due to the agitation caused by resting in the wonder of the "I-consciousness," its state of being like a non-existent thing is held to depend upon that [consciousness]. (3.103)
That repose within the Self of Maheśa, which consists of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā), even that manifests (or proceeds toward) a supreme state through its subtle differentiation. (3/104)
That is the abode of the Goddess, wherein the Lord, though [otherwise] bewildered as to his direction, becomes established;
for within that Light, both existence and non-existence attain their foundation. (3.105)

And that [consciousness] also resides within the wonder of consciousness, which is devoid of all dependence, and from which the piercing impact of the latent impressions of gradations and the like has long since departed. (3.106)
At the conclusion of the repose in the Other, that [consciousness] also comes to rest of its own accord; for they remain even in the state of repose within the supreme light. (3.107)
The impregnations, impulses, and latent traces consist of existence, non-existence, and both;
therefore, having rendered them into a state of non-being, that which is the unsurpassed repose [is the goal]. (3.108)
That goddess is so called; her method is the "method of the deity" (*devatā-naya*).
Since the *ṭaṅka* [measure] is exhausted even on that non-clothed [canvas], therefore it is the "method" (*naya*) from that. (3/109)
That which is the repose within the devouring of time is the form of the Supreme Lord;
whereas that which is the repose of repose is held to be the form of the Goddess. (3/110)
Thus, this subtle distinction between the two Supreme Lords, though they are one, has been clearly demonstrated for the sake of purifying one's understanding. (3.111)
Thus, since the universe in every respect depends upon cognition both for its manifestation and for its being known, how could there be the doubt as to how its prior origination occurred? (3.112)
In order to sever [the bonds], the Wheel of Vyomeśvarī is clearly revealed here—beautiful with the essence of its radiance within the ocean of unobscured consciousness. (3.113)
That wherein the repose of the manifestation of the other comes to rest by itself—that is the form of the Goddess here within, as the nature of the first vibration. (3.114)
The wheel consisting of the five [elements], arisen as the seed-syllable of the universe, is devoid of all dependence and has the nature of its own spontaneous vibration. (3.115)
Even there, another consciousness-space is superior to the other spaces; it consists of that [space], yet transcends it, existing as all-pervasive. (3.116)
She who is of the nature of the first creative intuition (pratibhā) is called this Vyomeśī;
that which is the essential form of Khecarī and the others is merely her own unfolding. (3/117)

Each [deity] is adorned with the five goddesses in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*); yet, due to the predominance of the overflowing splendor of their absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), they are spoken of separately. (3/118)
In the place where there is the experience of sound and so forth, consciousness (saṃvit) takes on the form of vibration and the like;
it is experienced individually through its own appropriate subtle function. (3/119)
In this way, in every single object, the entire circle of goddesses shines forth as the essence of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya), augmented by the fivefold experience. (3.120)
Thus, the universe, consisting of the five elements, is established by one's own experience;
it was previously described as being of the nature of the five spaces within the self of consciousness. (3.121)
The pentad of powers beginning with consciousness (cit) is [described] due to the predominance of the illumination of the other;
however, this [subsequent group] is intended [to be described] due to the predominance of resting in the rest within the Supreme (para). (3/122)
Pervasiveness, eternality, fullness, omniscience, and omnipotence—this is the definition of the fivefold power. (3.123)

The attainment of its own nature by the universe occurs first as consciousness, and after that, as accomplishment (*siddhi*) due to the excellence of knowledge; however, that [attainment] is characterized solely by pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). (3.124)
Thus, the structure of the universe first manifests as the nature of consciousness, and subsequently as the nature of the individual soul, by virtue of its own essence as the Supreme Power. (3.125)
Consisting of the sequence of bindus that are the manifestation of self-luminous bliss, it exists as the expansion of the five wheels (cakras), composed of Vyomeśī and the others. (3/126)

Although this [reality] is non-sequential, it appears as sequential on the plane of instruction, because of the demonstration of the distinctions between the various diversities of its respective perceptions. (3.127)
That very form of consciousness, manifesting as fivefold through its nature of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya), is first called the wheel of Vyomeśī. (3.128)
And this true nature of the Guru is that which pierces all veils and is entirely intent upon the immersion of resting in the supreme nature. (3.129)
By the mere knowledge of this, the veils of the body and so forth are destroyed;
through its worship, however, there is firm growth [of realization]. Therefore, it is indeed the most worthy of worship. (3.130)
By means of this description of the first wheel of Vyomeśvarī, which is the cause for attaining the entirety of the world's splendor, the wise,
having gained focused attention, shall enjoy [the fruits].
Those who are established in the Supreme Self abide in the state that is devoid of beginning and end.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of Vyomeśvarī," in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Having understood the undivided nature of the seed-syllable, which is the source for the expansion of the play of various experiences and which contains its own internal logic, we shall expound the sequence of the wheel of light. (4.1)
That which is known as one's own fivefold wheel, consisting of consciousness, is considered to be twofold in each case, by virtue of its nature as both knowledge and action. (4.2)
Established within the two groups of the organs of cognition and action as the very essence of knowledge and action, they are clearly tenfold because their core consists of attainment. (4.3)
When the intellect and the mind abide in their substratum in a general form, there exists this twelvefold group whose nature consists of the turbidity of light. (4.4)
Arising as non-differentiated, consisting of the non-conceptual, the first [wheel] is the object of worship for the circle of light, abiding in twelve ways. (4.5)
(22) It resides in the cave of the multitude of cognitions and is frequented by the perfected ones;
it exists by name according to its literal meaning, because of the predominance of pure luminosity alone. 4/6.

In this context, the rays of consciousness, which are inclined toward the creation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), are to be known by those whose wealth is attentiveness for the sake of purifying the twelve-fold self. (4.7)
This mass of rays, whose nature is a condensed light,
is the ground for the creation and dissolution of space, time, action, form, and the subtle divisions of manifestation.
The sequence of time, consisting of twelve parts such as the months and the signs of the zodiac, is experienced externally, enveloped by the manifestation of various respective states. (4.9)

In these rays of light, which are intent upon the frantic activity of creating objects of perception, the ego-sense remains concealed and established therein, directed toward the external world. (4.10)

Because its primary nature is internal vibration within the unobstructed self of the void, the expansion of Khecarī occurs through the twelvefold [breath] as she moves indeed within that space. (4.11)
Due to the nature of power (*śakti*) consisting of the equilibrium of knowledge and action, the universe first comes into being by virtue of having that [power] as its form. (4.12)

Then, by way of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there arises a twelvefold nature, characterized by a slight swelling [of consciousness] due to the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between knowledge and action. (4.13)
For yogis who have fixed their attention here upon the self consisting of place, time, and action, there occurs the sudden swallowing of the sequence of time. (4.14)
Those which exist for the world as obscurers of its own nature are, for the wise, the expansion of their own true form. (4/15)
Therefore, this twelvefold emergence of the sequence of time is itself the earth, suddenly swallowed by that which is thus situated at its end. (4.16)
Thus has been described the wheel of illumination, which has entered the stage of direct experience through the application of noble reasoning,
and which is to be understood through the oral tradition from the mouth of the supreme guru.
It should be unwearied for those possessing the supreme meditative concentration. || 4/17 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of Radiance," in the *Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa*.
Now begins the fifth chapter. (p.
23) Those [powers] which shine forth through an expansion corresponding to their own will, consisting of a full state fashioned from the nature of their own self as the object of knowledge...
We shall now proclaim this very Wheel of Bliss (ānandacakra), in which there are rays of consciousness and indeed wonders. 5/1
The wheel of manifestation that was previously defined through the means of valid cognition fulfills its pervasive will, which consists in the power of the enjoyment of objects. (5.2)

And that form of the elements consisting of the subtle essences (*tanmātra*), which consists of the solidification of consciousness and is fivefold, is experienced as the very nature of the object. (5.3)

Therein, for the rays of consciousness consisting of the organs of cognition and action, once their establishment in non-conceptual [awareness] has been fully realized through the enjoyment of objects, [the state of liberation arises]. (5.4)
When the intellect and the mind are unified, that effort which was elevenfold becomes sixteenfold in nature through the fulfillment of the enjoyment of sense objects. (5/5)
This very wheel of bliss exists as a sixteenfold nature, jagged with the delineation of objects of knowledge through the wondrous play of the rays of consciousness. (5.6)

For that which constitutes the making of [the self] an object of knowledge, without abandoning its own essential nature, is characterized by the demonstration of a sovereignty difficult to achieve for itself. (5.7)
Because the objects of desire are fulfilled in every respect by this [wheel], and because it consists primarily of great bliss, the wheel is designated as "Bliss" (Ānanda). (5.8)
Even in this regard, for those possessed of wisdom who have fixed their minds [upon this], these very sense objects shall become the ground of the nature of consciousness. (5.9)

In this context, because the nature of the universe is fully realized in all its aspects, even the withdrawal (saṃhāra), which consists of relishing (carvaṇā), is declared as being inseparable [from that realization]. (5.10)

When the internal burden of the world has been brought to completion through the intensification of the activity of *sāmarasya*, the longing for the enjoyment of sense objects ceases, like that of mirages. (5.11)

When she has become the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*) and has arisen within this ground whose nature is will (*icchātman*), the expansion of that very ground—which moves [within it]—consists of sixteen aspects. (5.12)
The nature of one's own experience, as it arises within the wheel of bliss (ānandacakra), has been demonstrated;
may it always serve the great multitude for the attainment of meditative absorption (samādhi) through the enjoyment of their inner disposition. 5/13
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of Bliss," in the Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa.

Now begins the sixth chapter. (p. 24) In this [state], through the power of repetition, there occurs the dissolution of the rays—which consist of the enjoyment of the manifestation of the universe's glory—into the most unartificial form of the *ahaṅkāra*.

Having meditated upon that which has mastered the activity of the entire collection of the various divisions of time, the appropriate cycle of forms is now being explained through reasoned arguments. 6/1.
This wheel of bliss, which has been described as consisting of sixteen aspects, is said to find its rest in the subject through its return [to that source]. (6.2)
Therefore, the corporeality of the subject—the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) which consists of the state of being the goal of all practical activity—is experienced here. (6.3)
When the outward-facing rays are predominant, that unmanifest ego which exists becomes clearly established here in embodied form. (6.4)

Since he first exists as the twelvefold form of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he is the expansive manifestation of the emission of time, intensely radiant with consciousness like rays of light. (6.5)
By means of desire, which consists of the enjoyment of sense objects, this [world] is filled; for the world is essentially composed of time and desire when it is oriented toward the external. (6.6)

When the form of the world has been fully manifested, consisting of the sequence of time and desire, while the rays of light are despondent due to the expansion of the enjoyment of sense objects; || 6.7 ||
Intent upon the manifestation of the merging of his own essential nature through the process of reversion, he is the seventeenth leader of the sixteen rays. (6.8)
The ego, whose nature is that of the knower, has arisen as a formal manifestation;
let this wheel of forms, consisting of seventeen principles, be contemplated. (6.9)
Constantly intent on the audacity of devouring the self at the time of enjoying sensual pleasures,
it reaches the ground of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is the locus of the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those respective perceptions.
That which was formerly an outward-turned self, a mass of rays,
has now entered into the vessel of the Mother’s union (mātṛmelā).
The measure consisting of the creation of time is the cognition, and the object of measurement consists of desire and action;
where these two are dissolved and exist in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya), [that is the Supreme]. || 6.12 ||
This very channel for the swallowing of time exists in the form of the seed-state;
through impregnation (*āvāsanena*), it is suddenly experienced within the wheel of forms (*mūrticakra*). (6.13)
From time arises the expansion of desire, and from desire time increases;
thus, in the process of the universe's evolution, time and desire are merely causes, not ultimate realities.
Without being characterized by desire, how could time be of the nature of conceptualization?
And apart from the nature of conceptualization, how could desire possibly arise? (6.15)
Therefore, time and desire, which are mutually dependent, are not ultimately real; they have arisen from a form that is not delimited by time and from that which is free from desire. (6.16)
Where the devouring of those two occurs clearly through reversal, that is the essential nature of the Supreme Lord, which delights in swallowing the universe. (6.17)
Having pursued these objects of knowledge, Hara, assuming a massive form, consumed with his flames that pair consisting of Time and Desire, which was external to him. (6.18)
Thus, that very ego which is the creator of time and desire, through its reversal, is itself the internal destroyer of time and desire. (6.19)
Because of the predominance of the formal nature of the ego (ahaṅkāra), it is called the "Formed" (mūrti);
this wheel consists of seventeen [principles] and is beautiful through the union of the stages of manifestation. (6.20)
Because cognitions are by their very nature so diverse, the wheel of [conventional] usage proceeds with respect to the distinction between names and forms. (6.21)
Because the primacy belongs to its own established nature, it abides there as something already accomplished;
through its connection with that which is to be produced, its manifestation occurs by way of being a Yoginī due to its power. (6.22)
The supreme secret has been told here and there, bit by bit;
out of fear of danger, it is not revealed entirely in one place. (6.23)

In this *Mahānaya-prakāśa*, for those who understand the preceding and the following [sections], the reality of things shines forth as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand. (6.24)
Thus has the structure of the universe, ending with the subject, been described for the purpose of severing the doubt and fear of those who have become vessels for the glance of the Guru. (6.25)

In due order, as the forms of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, the universe has issued forth externally from the wheel of the void, by virtue of its nature as the Supreme Power. (6.26)
This very thought remained in the mind of the author of the hymn when he sang:
"Consciousness [is realized] through hymns, by means of perception, the means of knowledge, the object, and the knower. (6.27)
This expansion of the Goddess Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī is perfectly consistent, for she performs even the devouring of withdrawal by means of her return [to the source]. (6.28)

Through the excellent tradition of the Mūrticakra, may consciousness here—which consists of the shattering of time on all sides—shine forth for the supreme yogis as the ground of incomparable courage. (6.29)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheel of Embodiments," in the *Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa*.
Now begins the seventh chapter. (p.

27) Within which [the Supreme Reality], the entire multitude of cognitions—both non-conceptual and conceptual—along with their succession and consisting of arising and so forth, dissolves incessantly through the process of forceful digestion (*haṭhapāka*). 7.1.
Having experienced, through the grace of the Guru, that unsurpassed state of supreme rest, this very cycle of the Vṛndakrama is indeed said to be preceded by the collective assembly. (7.2)
Relying upon direct experience, the world—composed of the elements of past and future—was previously explained by the Guru through the perspective of the *pīṭha-krama*. (7.3)
Through the exclusion of any other cause, its emergence from the root occurs;
having emerged as the nature of the wheel of space, it is then revealed as fivefold. (7.4)

Furthermore, the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which consists of the clear activity of knowledge residing within its own self-luminous [nature], is established as being twelvefold. (7.5)

Beyond even that, due to the wonder of the perfection of sovereignty which is difficult to accomplish, the sixteenfold object of knowledge (*prameya*) known as Bliss (*ānanda*) has been described. (7.6)
Then, when the satisfaction derived from sovereignty over external objects has ceased, he remains established in his own self-sustaining state as the essence of both creation and withdrawal. (7.7)
Furthermore, it is through this process of reversion that everything dissolves;
from this seventeenth [element], the Mother, there arises the manifestation of form. (7.8)
Thus, in the course of the state of worldly transaction for all living beings, every external object that is established is essentially composed of the omniscient Self. (7.9)

Whatever exists here—consisting of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower—even if it appears to be established externally, cannot be established for anyone in any way without Light. (7.10)
Therefore, the manifestation of anything whatsoever occurs through the manifestation of [consciousness];
yet, because the one depends upon the other, there is no identity between the conscious and the insentient natures. (7.11)

Therefore, whatever variety of the universe is experienced as having an insentient nature, that which consists of its own internal traces, lines, and configurations is in fact independent and of the nature of consciousness. (7.12)
From the supreme space, through vibration, and then from will—in this sequence—the manifestation of objects subsequently proceeds by way of the sense organs. (7.13)
Even when an object is established externally, it exists for cognizers by their very nature;
therefore, in this regard, [the teacher explains] as far as the emergence and subsistence of the universe through the Guru. (7.14)
Withdrawal and one's own essential nature are shown through the state of being one's own witness;
therefore, there is everywhere an exposition of the true nature of the wheels. (7.15)
Through the empowerment of the Great Power, a state of equilibrium proceeds perpetually by means of this much, according to the analogy of a waterwheel and its buckets. (7.16)

The creation and destruction (or cyclic existence) of the world, consisting of being and non-being, remain established; even through the application of manifold sequences, they are projected beyond the range of [ordinary] perception. (7.17)
The continuous process of diverse creation and dissolution revolves;
for that which begins from the void and ends with the body is essentially of the nature of contraction, as previously described.
That is saṃsāra, while liberation is the reversal of its essential nature;
therefore, as long as saṃsāra exists, it remains in those various forms. (7.19)
Liberation does not come from the renunciation of existence, nor from the enjoyment of existence. (7.20)
Nor is it based on meditative cultivation, because one perceives only emptiness;
nor is it real for anyone, whether through non-grasping or grasping. (7.21)
That liberation which is essentially an uncontracted garment is the ultimate liberation;
in relation to which all other liberations within saṃsāra are considered inferior. (7.22)
This dissolution of one's own nature within the Self, through the practice of shattering all contraction, leads to the ground where latent impressions (vāsanā) come to rest. (7.23)
Therefore, for the sake of attaining that state which is free from obscuration, the structure of the sequence of the Vṛnda is described here through the grace of the Guru. (7.24)

Through the focused attention of one's own self-reflection, the existence of the entire universe, from the fire of universal destruction up to Śiva, is suddenly gathered within one's own essential nature. (7.25)
Those who propound the non-duality of Mahānaya, Mahāyāna, and Vedānta are shown to be similar to the Cārvākas who propound non-duality. (7.26)
Those objects which are distinct from one another according to the analogy of the elephant and the gnat are nevertheless deceived by dull-witted people through similar designations. (7.27)
Therefore, having established the principle of nihilism in their minds, those evil-souled ones bring about the ruin of themselves and others through this great instruction of the system. (7.28)
Even for the great-souled Śiva, whose nature is supremely exalted, the latent impression of contraction persists; what then need be said of other living beings? (7.29)
Therefore, through constant attentiveness, by remaining established in one's own true nature,
liberation while living (jīvanmukti) shines forth by virtue of overcoming the crocodile of all grasping.
And that attentiveness arises from the thorough cultivation of the nature of the subject, through the state of stability consisting of both non-conceptual and conceptual thought. (7.31)

For that which consists of cause and effect is indeed bound by the chains of conceptual construction, and is nourished by the piercing force of various kinds of grasping, knots, and latent predispositions. (7.32)
Indeed, it cannot be denied because it is known through individual self-awareness;
therefore, how could this [world] exist without that which has the nature of withdrawal? (7.33)
He can be swallowed up suddenly by means of subtle conversations alone;
therefore, [one should proceed] with firmness of one's own nature, which pierces all veils.
The supreme yogi should remain in the form of supreme attentiveness;
therefore, whatever has come forth through whatever means during the establishment of the universe. (7.35)
Through that very [means], the universe dissolves for him by means of forceful digestion (haṭhapāka), because it is dependent upon light and is, in reality, identical with it. (7.36)
Just as one establishes emptiness by means of the natural flow of consciousness, so too [does one do so] through the process of reversal by means of forceful maturation (*haṭhapāka*). (7.37)
Through the cultivation of its formal structure, it is possible to lead [the mind] to a state free from obscuration;
when this is correctly understood, there is liberation from the plane of saṃsāra. (7.38)
Otherwise, the nature of liberation would be nothing other than the way of saṃsāra, just as the universe exists and remains exactly as it is experienced. (7.39)
Through the dissolution of contraction and its structural form, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) shines forth;
exactly as they perceive the universe, so does it transform. (7.40)
Due to the sovereignty of consciousness, it abandons all concern for means;
therefore, this [consciousness], whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), manifests as the essence of speech. (7.41)
The true tradition has been transmitted by the Guru, who pierces all veils;
for within the wheel of forms, the ego arises as the nature of the subject. (7.42)
Through the forceful digestion [of all things] preceded by the withdrawal of the contraction of one's own self,
[he effects the dissolution] of the entire multitude of rays consisting of the latent impressions of objective phenomena from every side.
Abiding in the form of the seed within the mother’s womb, [he perceives] the portions of non-conceptual and conceptual thought that follow after the duality of existence and non-existence. (7.44)
Having repeatedly pierced through [the layers], he withdraws even the internal [elements];
the portions of non-conceptual and conceptual [states] generally [merge] by virtue of their integration. (7.45)
Sixty-four types of cognition arise by their very nature;
among these, there are cognitions whose forms consist of mastery over the knowable and the formative forces. (7.46)
Sixty-four [types] arise through the application of the sequence of steps; others, moreover, are fixed upon that [state], being solely intent on the "forceful cooking" (*haṭhapāka*). (7.47)
In reality, they are precisely as many as the cognizer and the objects of experience;
they are a cluster of rays whose nature consists of the cognizer and the objects of experience. (7.48)
Therein, each [element] exists in order to swallow by means of forceful digestion;
and that exists both in a manifest and unmanifest state, as is known from experience. (7.49)
Due to the sequence of cognitions whose forms are the impressions of the objects of knowledge, the characteristic of all these cognitions is their final rest in the Supreme. (7.50)
That form which does not fall away for even a moment is the ultimate reality;
it transcends all, consists of all, and is the manifestation whose nature is the totality of everything. (7.51)
That certain supreme state of the Lord, which is undivided yet appears as if divided,
transcends all designations because it abides in its own essential nature.
The state of being sixty-five cognitions is proclaimed metaphorically;
this expansion of Raudreśvarī is established as the primary principle. (7.53)

Consisting of the forceful digestion of conditioned impressions (saṃskāra), having reached the further shore of the activity of devouring, it indeed exists as that which extends from the form of the Devourer of Destruction (saṃhārabhakṣiṇī) down to Vyomeśī. (7.54)
Within the sequence of its own innate wheels, this wheel-formation, having divided its own form, consists of the process of forceful ripening (*haṭhapāka*). (7.55)
Upon returning to one's own nature, which is beautiful and free from obscuration, consciousness—
devoid of volition and mental impressions— comes to rest spontaneously once it has been exhausted.
This slender-bodied Goddess is the ground where all desires dissolve; she is the ultimate state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya) attained upon ascending the supreme stream. (7.57)
In order to attain the state beyond falling back, some worship her by means of the appropriate method, entering into whichever Cakreśvarī resides within their own respective wheel. (7.58)
Raudreśvarī herself devours all the wheels from their very root;
therefore, in the Vṛndakrama, everything exists as something to be accepted. (7/59)

The entire range of objects of knowledge is capable of severing the slightest trace of contraction, because it establishes objects of knowledge such as mudrās, mantras, and the effortless state. (7.60)
Through discourse, the self attains the highest steadfastness in this tradition;
through discourse, doubt is severed; worship leads to perfection. (7.61)
From the transition [of consciousness], the supreme culmination of equanimity proceeds;
therefore, let this be reflected upon here with an attentive heart. (7.62)
The sixty-fourfold arrangement of rays is heart-pleasing;
through direct experience, all this becomes one's own self for yogins. (7.63)

Therefore, that which is experienced through direct perception from the mouth of the Guru is the manifestation of desire, which consists of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the enjoyment of sense objects. (7.64)
In time, that [karma] is again encountered through the sequence of its seed;
and when the satisfaction of time has ceased even by means of experiencing that [result], [the fruit ripens]. (7.65)
In due order, a clear loss of their own essential nature arises.
Thus, having first created desire, that [time] proceeds from there in sequence. (7.66)
But by returning [to its source], through the swallowing of that [object], it swallows each of its own respective forms;
in reality, all this is but the manifestation of mirages. (7.67)
For those things that are without succession, the form in which succession appears exists as something not directly perceived;
therein, the emanation of time, consisting of twelve aspects, has been described. (7.68)
Through the process of returning and measuring, by merging with the embodied ego,
she attains a thirteenfold nature while remaining oriented toward the state of ultimate rest.
Through the arising and so forth of each of the thirteen forms, there are fivefold [aspects];
thus, these sixty-five are the rays of light. (7.70)
The final [state] is sung of as the repose resulting from the transcendence of both sequence and non-sequence;
it is the culminating ground of the equilibrium of the sixty-four rays. (7.71)
The rays of the twelve-fold self, which consist of the splendor of the rising [of the sun] and so forth,
have forms that follow the supreme ego-consciousness consisting of that very splendor.
Those who are greedy for devouring by force proceed toward every state of being,
for they exist within the intermediate self that is the ground of the experience of all things.
The wheel of the rays of all the sense-faculties shines forth simultaneously; wherever and in whatever form or object each faculty possesses its specific jurisdiction.
In each respective case, only its own predominance exists there;
it is not that the others are dissolved within it, were it not for this single experience. (7.75)
How could there be a desire for another woman, so rich in the bloom of her beauty and charm?
For such a desire is generally of the nature of the sense of touch. (7.76)
And here, there is no play of form or beauty consisting of touch;
likewise, there is no sweetness of speech, nor the fragrance of the limbs or the breath. (7/77)
And the drinking of the nectar from the lower [mouth] would all be fruitless;
thus, in this way, there is the state of being the self of everything for all the rays. (7.78)
Established in the state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya) through the satisfaction of the subject, he is this supreme hero, characterized by the supreme ego (parāhaṃkāra). (7.79)
Having attained the primordial sacrifice, characterized by the supreme melting away of all rays simultaneously, it exists in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
This very Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara), immediately following the primordial sacrifice, is united within with the wheel of powers consisting of sixty-four [deities]. (7.81)

The formative impressions (saṃskāras), whose nature consists of both the non-conceptual and the conceptual, take the form of a bound soul (paśu); yet even they are dissolved through complete rest in the throat.
She strikes with force and impetuosity for the sake of satisfying her own wheel;
and in the center, she consists of the essence of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the wonder of supreme bliss. (7.83)
A certain intoxication expands, manifesting as a tumultuous activity;
even this [activity], when confronted by the supreme power, falls into a state of fleeing in all directions.
This Goddess, seated upon the hero’s throne, is the supreme auspiciousness; she arises from the movement of the form of delusion and from the treading upon supreme consciousness. (7.85)
The Guru is the master of all wheels, transcending both the sequential and non-sequential stages;
he is established in a twofold manner as both the illumination and that which transcends it. (7.86)
One [aspect] is oriented outwardly, consisting of the vibration, will, vision, and action of the supreme space;
the other is distinct from that sequence and is established in the supreme space.

Even though it is extroverted, there is a relishing [of the object] through will; that [relishing] consists of the triad [of will, knowledge, and action], and through contact with desire, it returns completely to the Self.
Furthermore, the swallowing of time through knowledge and action is also rest;
for that which is clearly manifest even in the non-conceptual state, once the enjoyment of objects has been fully known. (7.89)

For everyone, there is a momentary rest in the swallowing of time; however, when turned inward, due to the radiance consisting of the activity of the reflective awareness of objective phenomena, [there arises the state of Śiva]. (7.90)
Beginning from the arousal [of consciousness] up to its rest within the *citi*, this pentad remains established;
thus, at the occasion when there is an absence of outward orientation, there is indeed the arising and so forth. (7.91)
From the sequence of Vyomeśvarī up to the pentad of Raudreśī, that [sequence] rests externally, pervading the universe; now, [the teaching] concerning the nature of action (*kriyātman*) follows.
Through reflective discernment (*vimarśa*), that [reality] remains even as far as the supreme space;
its manifestation has been effected by the Guru in the form of various rituals such as sacrifice.
Consequently, the structure of the entire universe has been explained from its very foundation. (7.94)

Therefore, because it extends to the wheel consisting of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, the knower, and the self-form, [the author now explains] in what form everything, in all its aspects, dissolves. (7.95)
That host is presented in its very natural order, even though the state of equilibrium—characterized by the union of knowledge and the object of knowledge—has been attained. (7.96)
Since the impressions, impulses, and latent tendencies persist even during the dissolution of time, they cannot be removed without ritual action. (7.97)

In reality, through the immersion in action that proceeds by way of devouring [all things], one is fully established in the nature of the reflective awareness of consciousness, which consists of the sacrifice of one's own self. (7.98)
In particular, so that there may be no further emergence for these [souls],
he is the expansive Raudreśvarī, whose nature consists of supreme grace.

The transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of false pride (*mithyābhimāna*), dissolves here; the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose nature is desireless and free from mental constructs (*nissaṃskāra-prakāmātman*), proceeds forth. (7.100)
Therefore, the preeminence of this very goddess is also asserted, because from her the state of being free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇatā*) clearly arises. (7.101)
Previously, those cognitions which consist of the wall-like impressions of the objects of knowledge were described as sixty-four, in the form of a sequence of steps. (7.102)

(37) Within one's own wheel, the extraction by means of forceful ripening— through the nature of conscious reflection— of those [energies] in the form of bound souls, which consist of the three abodes.
Through the experience of the sequence of the *carucaryā* and other practices, one becomes stable therein;
first, among the sixteen-fold self, is the form of Raudreśvarī. (7.104)

It is the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cidvimarśa*) that has set out to lead the wheel of mental impressions—which consists of the enjoyment of objects—to a state of being free from obscuration. (7.105)
The very nature of desire has been swallowed here on all sides from its very root by means of the ego, which relies upon the established reality of those various rays. (7.106)
Having entered into the state of perfected selfhood—the gnosis whose form devours through withdrawal—the wheel of the latent impressions of the objects of knowledge dissolves therein. (7.107)

Then, [there arises] the cycle of mental impressions (mānasa-saṃskāra-cakra), which consists of twelve aspects, abides in the nature of time (kāla-svabhāva), and is characterized by the process of recirculation. || 7.108 ||

Through non-conceptualization and conceptualization, by way of the twenty-four forms, and by virtue of the two qualities of reflecting and protecting, [one attains] the nature of being composed of the accomplishment of mantra. (7.109)
Having entered that, the dissolution of the conceptualization of its own nature occurs;
having entered the form of Bhūcarī, it is performed through the nature of direct experience. (7.110)

Then, because that which has the form of conceptualization is established in the non-conceptual, one relies upon the perfection of the *melāpa* [conjunction] and the devouring of time (*kālagrāsa*) is indeed extended. (7.111)

Following the emergence of the sequence consisting of the twelve-fold melāpa, there arise the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) whose nature consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), as well as the three internal organs. (7.112)
In this context, eight Śākta [powers] are distinguished, whose forms are unmanifest;
through their extraction, the eightfold Śākta [power] is forcibly brought forth. (7.113)
Having entered the form of Khecarī, [the yogin] who discerns the divisions of subtle moments,
through the mode of subtle observation, [perceives] that which is supreme and consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

Even for a single person, there is the possibility of the impelling force of the latent impressions of desire; likewise, it exists for one who has reached the stage of the latent impressions of the three internal organs. (7.115)
Even for one who possesses penetration (*anuvedha*) and whose exertion is dissolved herein, that wheel of Śambhu exists in the form of a wheel, established through the sequence (*krama*). (7.116)
Since the manifestation of the supreme form of Śiva, which is of the nature of bliss (śam), occurs through this, it is therefore proclaimed as the Śāmbhava-cakra. || 7/117 ||
Vyomeśvarī, by means of the process of returning to her own essential nature,
enters the form of Raudreśī immediately after the swallowing of time (kālagrāsa).
Having performed its entire function, it naturally comes to rest;
therefore, in this regard, the entire wheel of mental formations is of a non-sequential nature.

Through the repeated practice of the objects of knowledge, [consciousness] manifests according to its respective degree of clarity or obscurity, consisting of sixty-four aspects in the form of the knower and the enjoyer. (7.120)

The state of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower, through their diverse sequential forms, will be established as the sixty-fourfold object of knowledge in all its aspects. (7.121)
In this very context, the tradition consisting of mudrās and mantras continues;
its essential nature is also explained here as an incidental matter. (7.122)
The configuration of the mudrās is intended to make known one's own essential nature;
protection by means of one's own self-reflection is intended as the defining characteristic of mantra. (7.123)
Even in states of worldly activity, which consist of various kinds of experiences, these two—of which the essence is pervasion—are clearly established through direct perception. (7.124)
Even now, because its nature remains undifferentiated, it exists as if beyond perception;
yet, by virtue of fully realizing it, phenomenal existence becomes the ground of liberation. (7.125)
The mudrā, the mantra, the bindu, and the nāda—whose nature is effortless and which rests upon that [Reality]—exist without division across all planes of experience. (7.126)
Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhinī, Bhairavī, Lelihānikā, and Khecarī—thus exists the fivefold nature of the mudrā. (7.127)
The sequence of that [Krama], according to its divisions into Jñāna, Mantra, Melāpa, Śākta, and Śāmbhava, is in every respect connected with these [five goddesses] in their respective order. (7.128)

For those who are effortless regarding mudrās and mantras, whose nature consists of the abode, the phonemes, and consciousness, there is non-differentiation due to their state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya) through mutual non-deviation. (7.129)
In this sequence, there exists some form of direct perception that extends up to the state of omniscience;
by virtue of its thorough knowledge, it pertains to the basis of body, speech, and mind. (7.130)
Through the dissolution of the latent impressions of contraction, [consciousness] becomes purified in every aspect;
it assumes the nature of the pervader of the three types of immersion, beginning with the individual (āṇava).

Even where, due to distinct experiences, there may be for the sake of abiding in one's own nature a triad of impurities—beginning with *yādi*, *karma*, and so forth—in a sequential manner of dissolution; 7.132.
By whose grace and by whose expansion the grinding of time is cast off, [and] by the fulfillment of His will, everything is emitted from the Fire of Time up to Śiva. (7.133)
Even now, this object of knowledge has not emerged from the state of being described as mere manifestation;
it has been transmitted only to a few, passing sequentially from mouth to mouth. (7.134)
Without which there would be no statement of its great purpose, regardless of its nature;
and without which no distinctiveness would arise for this system of reasoning. (7.135)
This very [teaching], because it is of a secret nature, has as its sole domain the oral tradition;
it cannot be properly inscribed even slightly in writing by one's power. (7.136)
