That knowledge of those who perceive the subtle is directed toward the intellect;
for, through the direct experience of this [intellect], the grasping of duality is indeed overcome with effort. (7.137)

For cognizers who are by nature devoid of color, form, and configuration, [the state] exists through the absence of cloth, chisels, and conventions, established by virtue of bodily configuration. (7.138)
And that mudrā, consisting of the form of the body’s configuration, is considered universal;
because its nature is the experience of the skull-bowl (karaṅka), it is first [manifested] as Sākaraṅkiṇī. (7/139)
Then, by virtue of the skeleton-form being established within his own self, he persists by assuming the form of the Wrathful Goddess through intense fervor. (7.140)
Furthermore, because she appropriately provides the sustenance for that very nature which revolves within [the self], she is proclaimed as Bhairavī. (7.141)

Furthermore, because it dissolves even that [state]—the eightfold city of the form of latent impressions (vāsanā)—and because its nature is that of the Great Dissolution (mahāvilaya), it is called Lelihāna. (7.142)
Then, when [the Self] has attained establishment in its own true nature (*svasvarūpa*), it assumes the form of *khecarī* because its nature is free from obscuration. (7.143)
This is that supreme mudrā, extending from the netherworld (pātāla) up to Śiva; having satiated the entire world, she remains established in her own station. (7.144)
For such a state— consisting of both the moving and the stationary—
is projected within the inner nature of the expressive self in the form of mantra.
Through the act of reflective discernment (*parāmarśa*), it attains its own nature by virtue of being joined with protection;
thus, speech consisting of the unmanifested phonemes (*avarṇamaya*) remains in the form of conceptual construction (*kalpa*). (7.146)
The great mantra is of the nature of the letterless (*avarṇātman*), intent upon the veiling of the universe;
the world consists of the five mudrās within the resonance of its own essential form. (7.147)
Drawn forth and struck with force, it is released by the unstruck sound; it is the cessation of the proliferation of duality, reaching the ultimate limit of reflective awareness. (7.148)
Knowing these two to abide in a state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya), one finds rest in the form of effortless activity, which is characterized by supreme repose. (7.149)
In reality, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is indeed consciousness alone;
for even there, the state of being free from obscuration (nirāvaraṇatā) actually persists.
Time and desire are not real by virtue of their mutual dependence; yet it is not that they do not exist, since they appear within the path of cognition. (7.151)
Just as that very nature of the consciousness is unobstructed, why is it not likewise established through self-awareness for these two? (7.152)
However, that form which exists as appearing before one's face in these two cases is like the appearance of a mass of hair; yet, it is once again free from obscuration. (7.153)
Indeed, the persistence of these two is solely due to the fault of non-reflection;
reflection, however, O Goddess, is the ground for supreme grace. (7.154)
When conceptual grasping has arisen, whether it be movement or stillness, for the yogi these two are in reality equal. (7.155)
Arising from the friction of the two-fold thorough knowledge of this form, consciousness itself—devoid of activity and for one who has no further need—shines forth as the Self. (7.156)

Through this method, the state of being established in every single entity consists of the unity of the mudrās, mantras, and the effortless [deities], whose nature is the light, the phonemes, and consciousness. (7.157)
The description of the true nature of the mudrās, the form of the mantra, and the worship;
and the transition [of consciousness]—this triad is, for one whose self is free from desire, a single unity. (7.158)

The omnipresent one, whose nature is the mass of space consisting of the five voids, shines forth as the unborn essence of the phonemes, having taken recourse to the configuration of consciousness. (7.159)
The nature of the sixteen vowels resides within this [reality] in a manifest state;
it is merely not perceived due to the lack of the convention of the *apaṭāṭaṅka*. (7.160)

Through the power of this, the yogis' meditative absorption (samādhi) occurs during the state of emergence (vyutthāna), by virtue of an identical realization through the imitation of that which is to be imitated. (7.161)
The pervasive state exists with a single nature throughout all scripts;
other letters differ, but this [pervasive state] does not. (7.162)
The single nature of the mudrā, existing as the essence of the skull-cup, is the great universal characteristic extending from the individual soul (ākṣiti) up to Śiva. (7.163)
In the very same way, the King of Phonemes (varṇarāja), who is the embodiment of the Great Mantra,
exists as the nature of the universal sound that denotes all things.
Likewise, there exists the following of consciousness in the form of the wheel of space (khacakra).
Moreover, by virtue of its effortless nature, it is characterized by resting in these two. || 7.165 ||

Thus, this triad of concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi), by its very nature, remains present even during the state of emergence; when these three are unified in one place, it is called "mastery" (saṃyama). (7.166)
By virtue of thoroughly understanding this, there is in reality no distraction;
by not thoroughly understanding this very nature, what stages of distraction could there be? (7.167)
This supreme secret, residing in the mouths of the yoginīs, has been unveiled and imparted for fear that it might wither away through oral transmission alone. (7.168)
Whatever great offense has been committed by me through the disclosure of this, may that solar orb be forgiven to me by virtue of the Guru’s grace. (7.169)

The arrangement of the script for this very king of phonemes—which consists of the five *piṇḍas* and whose nature is the subtle progression of the vital breath—is otherwise [than previously described]. (7.170)
Relying upon supreme consciousness, it abides as the staff (or the essence) of the severed head;
it is the nature of the fire-drill consisting of phonemes, whose form arises from the consciousness of the heart.
Resounding with the supreme sound that expresses the Great Universal (mahāsāmānya), [it arises] below from the striking of the hood by the great whirlpool of the stream of Kuṇḍalinī. (7.172)
Through the accomplishment of its own pervasive form as sound (or resonance), it establishes its state;
yet, through its return, it consists in the withdrawal of the object of knowledge into its own abode.
For one who perceives [the reality] up to the limit of Amākalā, even beyond that,
in the supreme state which is the void-nature of the Bindu, there arises from that station the state of being free from obscuration.
Shaving [the head] consists of the nature of knowledge, and the staff consists of the nature of action;
therefore, the sequence of shaving and the staff are considered to have the nature of knowledge and action respectively. (7.175)
In the region of the head is the Self in the form of the *muṇḍa*, which is the support consisting of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*);
below that is another, the Self in the form of the *daṇḍa*, which consists of the expansion of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). (7.176)
The first is the nature of the vibration of Vyomeśvarī, oriented toward the emergence of the universe; the other consists of the expansion of Raudreśvarī, which dissolves the universe. (7.177)
The Mudrā, whose essence is pervasiveness and whose nature consists of the activity of the five vital breaths, abides as the embodied form of a certain Piṇḍanātha. (7.178)
Through the contemplation of Piṇḍanātha, who is the manifestation of the sequence of the subtle vital breath, the sudden dawns of yoga arise for yogins by virtue of its great power. (7.179)
Through direct experience, this supreme sovereign of the bodily form becomes the primary resting place for yogis, serving as the source of consciousness-bliss. (7.180)
The gross sequence is generally established as the essence of pervasion;
it is considered by yogins to be the form of those [powers] whose influence consists in the subtle sequence. (7.181)
Therefore, the utility of the Piṇḍanātha is also established here;
for him too, the experience consists in one-pointed concentration on the abode, the phonemes, and consciousness. (7.182)
When the time arrives to seize and swallow the body, then that very time is also conceived as the destruction of one's enjoyments. (7.183)
The light of consciousness shines forth in the form of a non-sequential utterance, by way of the vital process consisting of the differentiation between the signified and the signifier. (7.184)
This [phoneme], whose nature is sequential, is established as non-sequential in form;
furthermore, it exists as a universal by virtue of its proximity [to the non-sequential]. (7.185)

Thus, those who, abandoning their own direct experience, merely fill out the numbers by some means or other regarding the wheels (*cakras*), knots (*granthis*), supports (*ādhāras*), and digits (*kalās*), [are deluded]. (7.186)
Even those who loudly proclaim their own nature through the final letters of the sequence of phonemes and other improper methods are not possessors of true knowledge. (7.187)

Therefore, the sequences and other such matters that have been set forth here by those who know [the truth] regarding the non-proliferation of the *āṇava* state have not been elaborated upon by us. (7.188)
In this sequence of the Śākinīs, which shines forth from its very root,
he who is capable [of practicing it] is one from whom the arising of doubt has completely dissolved;
he is the tradition of those destined for liberation, established in direct experience.
May he be for the sake of satisfying [the soul] with the nectar-essence of its own bliss. || 7/189 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Bṛndā-cakra," in the Śrī Mahānaya-prakāśa.

Now begins the eighth chapter. We shall expound the method for setting forth great power, which is intent upon the knowledge of one's own self, and which follows the sequence established in the nature of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal. (8.1)

The arising of the Guru, whose nature is the manifestation of the form accessible through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), has shone forth through the lineages ending with Vṛnda and Krama; he is the destroyer of all doubts. (8.2)
Therefore, at the conclusion of the sequence of the *bṛnda*, the lineage of gurus is worshipped;
it brings about the thorough knowledge of one's own nature and performs supreme grace for others. (8.3)

Therefore, when the thorough knowledge of the self is perfected, one who is free from conceptual construction, yet pierced by the latent impressions of conceptualization, proceeds with the nature of worship. (8.4)

What is called "worship" is not merely that firm resolve which is formed with flowers and other offerings; rather, worship is indeed that [resolve] directed toward the non-conceptual great void with a heart full of reverence. (8.5)
Thus, because the true nature of worship has been established in its reality, worship is indeed non-conceptual when the power of one's own contraction has fallen away. (8.6)
Since the essence of worship exists as the five forms beginning with the *yoni*, in accordance with the wheel of space (*khacakra*) which has the nature of the five voids. (8.7)
In that regard, the source (*yoni*) is the repose of the great being (*mahāsattā*) within all forms of consciousness;
it is proclaimed as the nature of the Great Source (*mahāyoni*) by virtue of its identity with the *pika* (the supreme subject). (8/8)

Arising from the nature of the conch-source that revolves upon the plane of the objects of knowledge, she once again takes on the form of the state of her own essential nature through the process of returning. (8.9)
Renowned as being born from a lotus, she then attained her own repose in the supreme state and arose as one of divine birth.
Thus, in brief, that which is the reality of the fivefold flow is the emergence of worship, whose nature is the creation consisting of non-conceptuality.
Since his state is always established through the grace of Yuganātha, the sequence of worship consists of abiding in that very nature. (8.12)
Therein, the form of Vyomeśvarī exists as the essence of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), consisting of the state of being unobscured within that which has the nature of the five spaces. (8.13)
Capable of contracting and expanding its own limbs, which consist of the means and objects of knowledge, it has arisen as Kūrmanātha in the form of both the sky-farer and the earth-farer. (8.14)
Through the return of the object of knowledge, she assumes the form of the Great Reabsorption;
she arises as Meṣanātha in the form of Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī. (8.15)
In reality, the Śrīmacchanda is so called because its nature consists of the essence of existence;
it is proclaimed as the form of Rudra and Raudreśvarī. (8.16)
Thus, the pentad beginning with Vyomeśvarī stands as the essence of the pervasion of the Yuganāthas, entered by their invisible forms. (8.17)
Immediately thereafter, through the stabilization of non-conceptual consciousness, one attains the form of the deity by means of the unfolding of one's own sovereignty. (8.18)
The eleven Marīcīs, beginning with Buddhi, are intent on the destruction of the mind; this is the primary sequence of worship for dissolution. (8.19)
Thus, this non-conceptual sequence is intended for the wheels of emanation, descent, and withdrawal, which are the very nature of worship. (8.20)

In this state, for those whose mental dispositions have ascended [to the highest level], there occurs at all times—even during the occasion of emergence—a swallowing of time within the various planes of experience. (8.21)
Therefore, this worship, which exists as the knowledge of the Self, is the flower of the tree of instruction—captivating with the fragrance of consciousness. (8.22)
Following that as well, preceded by the swallowing of time (*kāla*) by all the functions, there arises the repose in the unconditioned, which consists of the transition [to the state beyond]. (8.23)
For those for whom supreme rest arises from the mere mention of it, they no longer require dependence upon the cycles of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal. (8.24)
Immediately after the sequence of the *vṛnda*, that [tradition] maintains an "ineffable" (*anākhyā*) wheel;
in their view, the triad of wheels beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is not worshipped at all. (8.25)
In our view as well, that [attainment] is held to have its meaning fully complete;
for it is through the power of mounting this [state] that spiritual efficacy proceeds. (8.26)
From the libation performed with the *Vīrāvalī* and other mantras born of this contemplation (*vimarśa*), there occurred for Vāmanavīrya the paralyzing of Viṣṇu and other such feats. (8.27)
Indeed, it is stated in the *Siddhasūtras* that through worship one attains the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*);
from the knowledge of the Self, the powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) proceed according to one's will. (8.28)
In narration, in worship, and likewise in battle, each naturally possesses a threefold nature; however, a distinction is recognized based on their predominance. (8.29)

By means of their own [ritual] acts— such as creation and the rest— which are characterized by the radiance of innate being, intent upon the knowledge of the Self, and which have reached the essence of immersion in consciousness;
[they are] gladdened by the vast nectar of bliss consisting of the complete, stainless, and beautiful immortal nectar.
May the multitudes of yogis rejoice, finding their delight in the consumption of the sacrificial offering that is the devouring of Time.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wheels of Emanation and the Others," in the Mahānayaprakāśa.

Now begins the ninth chapter (ullāsa). That which is manifested through the cycles consisting of the sequence of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal does not deviate even slightly from its own state, which consists of the attainment of rest.

Having entered that state where the expansion has transcended both sequence and non-sequence, that Wheel of the Inexplicable (anākhyacakra) is now perceived through appropriate sequences of reasoning as it undergoes transference. 9.1.
In this way, the discourse and other activities concerning the Guru, the Self, and the Deity remain perpetually in a state of liquefied oneness for oneself across all planes of experience. (9.2)
"Even though there is no difference [between them], it is said that a distinction among these is accepted on account of their predominance;
relying upon that, the object of knowledge is presented in a corresponding manner. (9.3)
For generally, attachment to sexual intercourse, liquor, and meat is observed among all living beings; indeed, it is especially so for some individuals in certain instances. (9.4)
If an impulsive zeal for their renunciation is instilled in them beforehand, that instruction will not take root in the mind even in the slightest degree. (9.5)
The minds of men, habituated to sense-objects through hundreds of previous births, are indeed turned away from them with difficulty, like an old ox from the crops. (9.6)
Thus, because of their mutual agreement, it is indeed difficult to abandon them, for they harbor malice even toward those who offer instruction. (9.7)
When that which is taught is preceded by the nature of enjoyment as it actually exists, the world’s ascension upon it arises, preceded by faith. (9.8)
Furthermore, since there is no single uniform nature [to manifestation], how could they be excluded from it?
How could that nature of manifestation differ up until its very existence? (9/9)
If difference is imagined, then this imagination is not rooted in reality; for their dissolution occurs through mere manifestation, and is not ontological.
And that [is attained] through many difficult practices over incalculable eons;
for there is no absence of radiance, because nothing else is perceived. (9.11)
If mere non-existence were truly non-existent, it would have to appear at all times;
therefore, neither reality nor unreality can exist without appearance. (9.12)
The manifestation of both reality and unreality occurs equally by virtue of one's own sovereignty;
however, within the framework of the process of rejection and appropriation, it is established in this manner. (9.13)
Therefore, its true nature is established as it actually exists;
this state, consisting of perfect knowledge, is called liberation while living (jīvanmukti). (9.14)
Indeed, my one essential nature exists by pervading the states of the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the knower, consisting of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. (9.15)
Due to the power of individual conceptualization in accordance with their own respective natures, they exist in four ways through the distinctions of emanation, maintenance, and so forth. (9.16)

That which is indeed established as fourfold through the arising [of the energies] ending with the "swallowing of time" (kālagrāsa), its repose is but one; therefore, there are thirteen goddesses here. (9.17)
Because of the preeminence of the Wheel of the Ineffable (Anākhyacakra), they remain as objects of worship;
among them, the last is their own repose, the supreme ground of great dissolution.
Emanation, descent, and withdrawal are established as having a sequential nature;
even that which is inexpressible and non-sequential possesses a sequential nature by virtue of being dependent upon them. (9.19)

Because of the reflective awareness of the non-sequential self, which consists of the coloring of succession, the swallowing and transition of time occur suddenly; thus it is intended [by the term *grāsa*]. (9.20)
For in whatever object the rays of consciousness move, there indeed resides the effortless vibration known as the Unnamed (Anākhyā). (9.21)
If manifestation occurs through effort, how could it be possible for one who is attached?
Manifestation would be unchewed; how then could it exist without being polished? (9.22)
Whatever sequence exists within the forms of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, in each of those instances, the Unnameable stands first as non-sequential. (9.23)
Even in this interval, there is a repose that is free from the states of succession and non-succession;
it abides as an inseparable concomitant, unassailable by the limitation of time.
If consciousness were not to flow forth toward another entity, how else could it [be said to] have a delimited nature, since it rests solely upon the form of that [object]? (9.25)
The manifestation [of blue] is indeed established as blue, and that manifestation is established in the chewing of the sesame seed;
if it were not established simultaneously, the cognition of blue would not be accomplished. (9.26)
If there were first the blue, then its appearance, and then its relishing, occurring through mutual exclusion, then the cognition of blue would not exist. (9.27)
The sequence is said to consist of the nature of temporal succession, arising from mutual exclusion;
yet no such cognition could exist, because of the distinction between the various appearing parts. (9.28)

For those who know that [reality] to be partless, through the experience of the unnameable state consisting of enjoyment, and upon the complete perfection of all experience, the course of worldly life is established. (9.29)
This sequence which is established as appearing directly before one's face—its division, according to experience, remains clearly inexpressible. (9.30)
In that regard, there is a fourfold division of the nature of the object of knowledge (*meyasvarūpa*):
first, the unmanifested manifestation (*akalitollāsa*), and after that, its enjoyment (*tatsambhoga*). (9.31)
From that [recollection] comes savoring (carvaṇa), and immediately after that, cessation.
Thus, even within the nature of the aesthetic emotion (mānasa), a fourfold division is possible. (9.32)
It is to be fully known according to its own appropriateness, and likewise in the form of the Mothers;
here, in every case, there is only one resting-place, free from all limiting conditions.
Through the power of the contemplative realization of these twelve goddesses, the non-conceptual state, clearly free from the latent impressions of conceptual thought, proceeds. (9.34)
But those who are addicted to women, through that very addiction, gradually enter completely into the state of being devoured by Time, which is without refuge. (9.35)
Some find rest in the supportless state merely by seeing [the teacher], others through the touch of his limbs, and still others through the arousal of the two organs. (9.36)
Thus, for those addicted to women, three stages of experience are observed;
when time dissolves, there is an unconditioned rest. (9.37)

Through the distinctions of emission, non-emission, and so forth, there are four deities of the Unnameable (anākhyā) who, resting upon the plane of the object of knowledge, remain intent on swallowing time. (9.38)
Because the root *kal* clearly carries the sense of "casting" (*kṣepa*), the word *Kālī* stands as a designation for the four goddesses through its conformity with its etymological meaning. (9.39)
Emission (*kṣepa*) consists of the outward-turning desire arising from the enjoyment of one's own consort;
it is established as the swallowing of time (*kālagrāsa*), because [the state of] that [desire] is subject to dissolution and so forth. (9.40)
Thus, whatever beings exist who are addicted to intoxicants, it is said that they are devoured by Time precisely through that very addiction. (9.41)

For him as well, who possesses the yoga of seeing, touching, and drinking, the occurrence of being swallowed by Time (Kālagrāsa) is clearly observed when [the vital energy] is drawn out through its intensity. (9.42)
When the essence of *śīdhu* has entered within—that which consists of the removal of differentiation—the aesthetic wonder attains stability even without contact with external objects. (9.43)
Through the expansion of the central ground of great enjoyment consisting of reflections, the four periods remain established by relying upon the ground of valid cognition. (9.44)

And due to the functioning of the root *kal* in the sense of "counting" sounds, the emergence of *kāla* (time) occurs in four ways, through the distinctions of maintenance, creation, and so forth. (9.45)
Thus, having entered the form of the cognizer of those who are addicted to meat—the grounds of intermediate relish—four Kālikās remain. (9.46)

For one who has realized the meaning of the *kalidhātu*, these stages—beginning with the comprehension of its meaning—are considered to be the intensification of vision, touch, enjoyment, and supreme delight. (9.47)
This fourfold sequence, consisting of withdrawal, emanation, and so forth, is established through the continuous experience of wonder in the enjoyment of women, wine, and meat. (9.48)
The "devouring by time" (kālagrāsa), which clearly persists for some time among those in distress, is one thing;
however, this other category of states (bhāvavarga) constitutes its further elaboration (parikara). 9.49
By this very logic, even there, the state consists of being swallowed by Time;
it is with this very intention that [one proceeds] for the realization of the Supreme Brahman. (9.50)
Lalanā, honey, and meat are especially worthy of worship as the foremost [offerings].
Thus, in this manner, among all states of being and in all grounds of experience— || 9.51 ||

Through the vision of the great purpose, even the swallowing of time is easily accomplished without effort, by means of the correct investigation of reality—that is, through the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena. (9.52)
"I salute the abode of the Self, which has attained the bliss arising from awakening"—according to the logic of the oral tradition of the Siddhas, this does not exist in reality at all. (9.53)
The nature of reality is that wherein this time exists as a conceptualization;
all this arrangement of the self consists of its own expansion. (9.54)
Thus, by the bliss arising from awakening, what time indeed is swallowed? And those twelve periods of time are intent upon the exertion of swallowing that [time]. (9.55)

When investigated in this manner, because of the certainty that "nothing exists," there is only one [reality] characterized by the experience of consciousness and insentient matter, and the subsequent cessation of that experience. (9.56)
The supreme Goddess is repose, free from the limiting adjuncts of time;
she is the abode of all consciousness, whether conceptual or non-conceptual. (9.57)

That which transcends the states of succession and non-succession, though its nature consists of the full manifestation of that [succession], is immovable and devoid of vibration, yet it partakes in the enjoyment of all vibrations. (9/58)
Even today, she remains directly manifest to everyone through her various faces, and is likewise characterized by diverse means such as worship and ritual transmissions. (9.59)
The ground for the dissolution of the forms of these twelve goddesses is the thirteenth goddess, who is indeed spoken of figuratively. (9.60)
That very [energy], existing as the object of worship for others by virtue of its worthiness to be accepted,
acquires the names of the thirteen goddesses according to their respective fitness and through a method that is heart-pleasing. (9.61)
By means of these designations, those garlands of mantra-syllables exist metaphorically,
because they have been perceived through the sequence of Kālikā.

(54) Regarding the manifestation of the assembly (*melāpada*), since it is here within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*), how can there be the existence of mantra? Or, even if it were directly perceived, how could that be so? (9.63)
Directly perceived as the King of Letters (A), it belongs to the level of bodily experience;
though consisting of five clusters, it is also the object of perception for those who see the subtle. (9.64)
The other mantra-syllables are in no way directly perceived;
rather, their activity occurs through metaphorical designation within the scope of the sequential process. (9.65)
Through the complete exhaustion of the impelling force of the latent impressions produced by various conceptual constructions, a supreme rest arises, free from all longing. (9.66)
Thus, regarding the subject of arousal, this sequence of worship stands manifest to all living beings within the spheres of the experience of existence. (9.67)
Those very states which others avoid because they are obscuring, by means of those same states, the supreme consciousness of the wise blazes forth in this manner. (9.68)
In accordance with this meaning, those verses which have been clearly explained by me in the *Stotrabhaṭṭāraka* [are as follows]. || 9/69½ ||
